overview: Gunditjmara people maintain a living relationship with Country in south-western Victoria. At Budj Bim, generations shaped waterways into an aquaculture landscape. The map's imported date range describes its snapshots, not the beginning or end of Gunditjmara society.

items.text: Builders used volcanic stone to redirect water through channels, weirs and dams. These connected structures trapped, held and harvested kooyang, the short-finned eel.
Aquaculture depended on knowledge of seasonal eel movement, water flow and wetland ecology. Water management and food production were linked practices.
Kurtonitj preserves stone house sites alongside eel traps, channels and trees used for smoking eels. Settlement and food processing belong in the same landscape.
Storytelling, dance and basket weaving transmit knowledge across generations. Fibre baskets also belong to the practical technology of eel harvesting.
A cultural weir restored traditional flows into Tae Rak after earlier drainage. Gunditjmara customary responsibilities and cultural connections continue today.
